content: The Society of Critical Care Medicine (SCCM), founded in 1970, is an independent, international, educational, and scientific organization. It serves a global membership of 14,000 individuals who are committed to delivering the highest quality care to critically ill and injured patients. The SCCM fulfills its mission by supporting research, providing education, and advocating for issues related to critical care medicine. In 1927, the first hospital-based infant care center for premature infants was established at the Sarah Morris Hospital in Chicago. During World War II, shock wards were created to care for injured soldiers. Between 1947 and 1948, the polio epidemic led to significant advancements in treating patients with respiratory paralysis. In Denmark, manual ventilation was performed using a tube placed in the trachea of polio patients. These patients, suffering from respiratory paralysis or acute circulatory failure, required intensive nursing care. In the 1950s, the development of mechanical ventilation facilitated the establishment of respiratory intensive care units (ICUs). Grouping critically ill patients together in these units allowed for more efficient care. In 1958, intensive care began in the United States when Dr. E. Dandy opened a three-bed unit for postoperative neurosurgical patients at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore. By 1968, most hospitals in the United States reported having at least one ICU. The SCCM was officially established in 1970 during a meeting of 29 physicians in Los Angeles, California. Dr. Max Harry Weil became the Society's first president. In 1972, Dr. Peter Safar, credited with pioneering cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), became the second president of the SCCM. In 1986, the American Board of Medical Specialties approved certification in critical care for four primary specialties: anesthesiology, internal medicine, pediatrics, and surgery. By 1997, there were over 5,000 ICUs operating across the United States. The mission of the SCCM is to ensure the highest quality care for all critically ill and injured patients. The organization envisions a future where all critically ill individuals receive care from integrated teams of dedicated experts, led by trained and present intensivist physicians. These multidisciplinary teams utilize knowledge, technology, and compassion to deliver timely, safe, effective, and efficient patient-centered care. The SCCM holds its annual international conference in January or February, attracting approximately 6,000 healthcare professionals, including doctors, nurses, and pharmacists, from around the world who specialize in critical care. The Society also organizes numerous other conferences, symposia, courses, and meetings to advance the practice of critical care medicine. The SCCM publishes several periodicals, including Critical Care Medicine, Pediatric Critical Care Medicine (PCCM), and Critical Connections. It also produces The iCritical Care Podcast, which serves as an innovative medium for communication and education in critical care. The Society collaborates with other organizations, such as the Canadian Journal of Anesthesia and the American Academy of Pediatrics, to publish guidelines and research that advance the field of critical care medicine.
